extracted.intended_audience: media researchers and students conducting content analyses of news/tabloidization
extracted.subtask_description: Operationalizing and coding 'soft news' / tabloidization across topic, focus, and style dimensions for content analysis of newspapers, TV newscasts, and online/social media. Includes specific indicators, coding values, and references to codebooks (Reinemann et al. 2012; Steiner 2016; Donsbach & Büttner 2005).

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic dimension (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes soft from hard news by political relevance or by classifying topics as hard (e.g., politics, sometimes economics) or soft (e.g., crime, sports, lifestyle, human interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most studies classify items by topic/section (e.g., politics = hard; sports, crime, human interest = soft). Alternative operationalization: assess the explicit presence of political relevance indicators (see 'political relevance' indicator). Use nominal coding for topic categories; reliability and category lists/codes often provided in study-specific codebooks (e.g., Steiner 2016).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political relevance (Reinemann et al., 2012)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four aspects indicate the degree of political relevance: (1) societal actors, (2) decision-making authorities, (3) policy plan/measure, and (4) actors concerned. For each aspect, presence (1) or non-presence (0) is coded; the combined presence indicates political relevance of the item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalization (Reinemann et al. 2012, p.237): 1) Two or more societal actors disagreeing on a societal issue (e.g., two parties, party vs NGO); 2) Decision-making authorities (legislative, executive, judiciary) involved or potentially involved; 3) Substance of a planned/realized decision, measure, programme related to the issue; 4) Persons/groups concerned by planned/realized decisions/measures. Level of analysis: article; Values: 0 (not present) / 1 (present); nominal measurement. See Reinemann et al. (2012) codebook (DOI: 10.1177/1464884911427803) for full coding instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic / topic category (Steiner, 2016)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorical variable assigning each item to a topic/section code (e.g., politics, economics, crime, sports, human interest); categories are then grouped into 'hard' (politics, economics) vs 'soft' (crime, sport, human interest) news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example coding scheme (Steiner 2016): 101-247 politics; 310-399 economy (hard news); 900 accident/catastrophe; 1000-1010 crime; 1100 human interest; 1200 sport (soft news). Level of analysis: article; nominal measurement. Report coder reliability (Steiner reports intra-coder Krippendorff's α=0.81, Holsti=83.3%). Codebook (German) attached to Steiner study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus dimension (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiates hard vs soft news by framing: whether coverage is episodic vs thematic, and whether it emphasizes individual vs societal consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two distinct indicators commonly used: episodic vs thematic framing (captures event-focused vs context/thematic reporting) and individual vs societal framing (captures personal/private meanings vs societal-level consequences). Use ordinal coding for framing scales; see Reinemann et al. (2012) for detailed code definitions and levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodic vs thematic framing (Reinemann et al., 2012)
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes whether the news item's focus accentuates episodes/case studies/events (episodic) or broad context/issues (thematic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition: Episodically focused items present an issue via a specific example/case (e.g., unemployment covered via one individual's plight). Values: 0 = pure/predominant episodic; 1 = mixed episodic and thematic; 2 = pure/predominant thematic. Level of analysis: article; ordinal measurement. Reliability: variable not tested in Reinemann et al.; codebook available in appendix (DOI: 10.1177/1464884911427803).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual vs societal framing (Reinemann et al., 2012)
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes whether a news item's focus stresses personal/private meaning/consequences (individual) or broader societal relevance/consequences (societal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values: 0 = pure/predominant focus on individual relevance/consequences; 1 = mixed individual and societal; 2 = pure/predominant focus on societal relevance/consequences. Level: article; ordinal measurement. Variable reliability not tested in Reinemann et al.; consult codebook (DOI: 10.1177/1464884911427803) for examples and coding rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style dimension (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns how news is presented; soft news styles are more emotional, subjective, narrative, personal, colloquial, and conflict-emphasizing compared to hard news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies analyse multiple style indicators (emotional reporting, personal reporting, colloquial/loose language, narrative presentation, emphasis on conflicts). Indicators are operationalized separately and can be combined into an overall style score. Selection of style indicators varies across studies; consult specific codebooks (e.g., Reinemann et al. 2012; Donsbach & Büttner 2005; Steiner 2016).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional reporting (emotional – unemotional) (Reinemann et al., 2012)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures the emotional presentation of information using verbal, visual or auditive means that arouse or amplify audience emotions (e.g., dramatization, affective wording, visual presentation of emotions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of emotional techniques: (a) dramatizing events as exceptional/exciting/thrilling; (b) affective wording/speech — superlatives, strong adjectives, present tense for past events, pronounced accentuation; (c) reporting on or visually presenting explicit expressions of emotions (hurt, anger, fear, joy). Measurement: typically a multi-level ordinal scale (e.g., 0 purely/predominantly emotional; 1 mix; 2 purely/predominantly unemotional). Some studies disaggregate verbal style (linguistic features) vs visual style (images showing emotions). Codebook reference: Reinemann et al. (2012) appendix (DOI: 10.1177/1464884911427803).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal reporting (personal – impersonal) (Reinemann et al., 2012)
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes the explicit appearance of the journalist's personal point of view: presence of reporters' personal impressions, interpretations, points of view or opinions within the news item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values: 0 = purely/predominantly personal; 1 = mix of personal and impersonal elements; 2 = purely/predominantly impersonal. Level of analysis: article; ordinal measurement. Variable reliability not tested in Reinemann et al.; refer to codebook for concrete markers of personal voice vs neutral reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colloquial / loose language (Umgangssprache) (Steiner, 2016)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures degree of colloquial language in the item (how informal/loose the language is).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale: 0 = not colloquial at all; 1 = little colloquial; 2 = strongly colloquial. Level: article; ordinal measurement. Steiner reports intra-coder reliability: Krippendorff’s α = 0.72 (interval), Holsti = 88.9% (nominal). Codebook (German) describes linguistic features to identify colloquialism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative presentation (news pyramid vs narration) (Donsbach & Büttner, 2005)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures whether a news item follows the inverted news pyramid (answering key W-questions at the start) or tells a story/narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5-point scale example (Donsbach & Büttner): -2 = news pyramid; -1 = ; 0 = neither/nor; 1 = ; 2 = narrative. (Scale ranges from news-pyramid style to narrative presentation.) Level: article; ordinal measurement. Use codebook for anchor descriptions and coding examples (Donsbach codebook available online).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on conflicts (Konflikthaltigkeit) (Donsbach & Büttner, 2005)
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes whether conflicts are mentioned and whether they are implicit or explicit (degree to which conflict is present and salient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values (German example): 1 = implicit conflict (apparent but not openly addressed); 2 = explicit conflict (openly addressed); 9 = no conflict. Level: article; nominal measurement. Codebook (Donsbach) provides examples; reliability reported for multi-coder studies varies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall news softening / tabloidization (multidimensional assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptualizes tabloidization as a multi-dimensional continuum across topic, focus, and style; the degree of overall news softening is assessed by combining indicators across these dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine indicators (topic category or political relevance; episodic/thematic and individual/societal framing; emotional, personal, colloquial, narrative, conflict emphasis) into an aggregate measure or profile of 'softness'. Studies differ in which indicators they include and weighting schemes; document chosen indicators, coding scales, and reliability. References: Esser (1999); Reinemann et al. (2012) meta-analysis provides recommended dimensions and operationalizations.
